The dynamics of a degenerate epidemic model with nonlocal diffusion and free boundariesThanks:  † School of Mathematics and Statistics, Lanzhou University, Lanzhou, Gansu 730000, P.R. China
‡ Department of Mathematics, Harbin Engineering University, Harbin, 150001, P.R. China
§ School of Science and Technology, University of New England, Armidale, NSW 2351, Australia.
∗Corresponding author (wtli@lzue.edu.cn)

Meng Zhao†, Yang Zhang‡, Wan-Tong Li† and Yihong Du§
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We consider an epidemic model with nonlocal diffusion and free boundaries, which describes the evolution of an infectious agents with nonlocal diffusion and the infected humans without diffusion, where humans get infected by the agents, and infected humans in return contribute to the growth of the agents. The model can be viewed as a nonlocal version of the free boundary model studied by Ahn, Beak and Lin [2], with its origin tracing back to Capasso et al. [6, 5]. We prove that the problem has a unique solution defined for all t>0t>0, and its long-time dynamical behaviour is governed by a spreading-vanishing dichotomy. Sharp criteria for spreading and vanishing are also obtained, which reveal significant differences from the local diffusion model in [2]. Depending on the choice of the kernel function in the nonlocal diffusion operator, it is expected that the nonlocal model here may have accelerated spreading, which would contrast sharply to the model of [2], where the spreading has finite speed whenever spreading happens [33].

Key Words: Epidemic model, nonlocal diffusion, free boundary, spreading and vanishing.

AMS Subject Classification (2010): 35K, 45G15, 92D25

1. Introduction

The spatial spread of epidemic disease is an important subject in mathematical epidemiology. In this paper we consider an epidemic model that describes the evolution of an infectious agents and the infected humans, where humans get infected by the agents, and infected humans in return contribute to the growth of the agents. In the model, the spatial movement of the infectious agents is described by a nonlocal diffusion operator, while that for the infective humans is ignored. The range of the infected area is assumed to be a moving interval [g⁡(t),h⁡(t)]⊂ℝ[g(t),h(t)]\subset\mathbb{R}, with its two end points representing the spreading fronts of the disease. Thus the model is a degenerate nonlocal diffusion system with free boundaries. We will show that the model has a unique solution defined for all time, and then determine its long-time dynamical behaviour.

The origin of the model is the following ODE system

(1.1) {u′​(t)=−a​u​(t)+c​v​(t),t>0,v′​(t)=−b​v​(t)+G⁡(u⁡(t)),t>0,\begin{cases}u^{\prime}(t)=-au(t)+cv(t),&t>0,\\ v^{\prime}(t)=-bv(t)+G(u(t)),&t>0,\end{cases}

proposed by Capasso and Paveri-Fontana [6] to describe the cholera epidemic which spread in the European Mediterranean regions in 1973. Here a,b,ca,\ b,\ c are all positive constants, u⁡(t)u(t) and v⁡(t)v(t), respectively, stand for the average population concentration of the infectious agents and the infective humans in the infected area at time tt. 1/a1/a stands for the mean lifetime of the agents in the environment, 1/b1/b represents the mean infectious period of the infective humans, cc is the multiplicative factor of the infectious agents due to the infective humans, and G⁡(u)G(u) is the infection rate of the human population due to the concentration of uu in the infected area. A basic assumption of the model is that the total susceptible human population is large enough compared to the infective population, and is assumed to be constant during the evolution of the epidemic.

In (1.1), the spatial factor is ignored. The corresponding spatial diffusion problem was subsequently considered by Capasso and Maddalena [5], where it is assumed that the infectious agents disperse randomly, and the mobility of the infective human population is small and thus neglected. This diffusive model has the form

(1.2) {ut=d​Δ​u−a​u+c​v,t>0,x∈Ω,vt=−b​v+G⁡(u),t>0,x∈Ω,∂u∂n+α​u=0,t>0,x∈∂Ω,u(0,x)=u0(x),v(0,x)=v0(x),x∈Ω¯,\begin{cases}u_{t}=d\Delta u-au+cv,&t>0,\ x\in\Omega,\\ v_{t}=-bv+G(u),&t>0,\ x\in\Omega,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial\textbf{\emph{n}}}+\alpha u=0,&t>0,\ x\in\partial\Omega,\\ u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\ v(0,x)=v_{0}(x),&x\in\overline{\Omega},\end{cases}

where Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N} is a smooth bounded domain, representing the epidemic region, and the function GG is assumed to satisfy

  1. (G1):

    G∈C1​([0,∞)),G⁡(0)=0,G′​(z)>0G\in C^{1}([0,\infty)),\ G(0)=0,\ G^{\prime}(z)>0 for ∀z≥0\forall z\geq 0;

  2. (G2):

    G⁡(z)z\frac{G(z)}{z} is decreasing and limz→+∞G⁡(z)z<a​bc\lim\limits_{z\rightarrow+\infty}\frac{G(z)}{z}<\frac{ab}{c}.

It is shown in [5] that the number

R~0:=c​G′​(0)(a+d​λ1)​b\tilde{R}_{0}:=\frac{cG^{\prime}(0)}{(a+d\lambda_{1})b}

is a threshold value for the long-time dynamical behaviour of (1.2): The epidemic will eventually tend to extinction if 0<R~0≤10<\tilde{R}_{0}\leq 1, and there is a globally asymptotically stable endemic state if R~0>1\tilde{R}_{0}>1, where λ1\lambda_{1} is the first eigenvalue of

−Δ​ϕ=λ​ϕ​ in ​Ω,∂ϕ∂n+α​ϕ=0​ on ​∂Ω.-\Delta\phi=\lambda\phi\text{\ in\ }\Omega,\;\;\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial\textbf{\emph{n}}}+\alpha\phi=0\text{\ on\ }\partial\Omega.

To describe how the epidemic spreads in space, one useful notion is the spreading speed. This can be achieved by considering (1.2) over the entire ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} instead of over a bounded domain Ω\Omega, coupled with initial functions (u,v)=(u0,v0)(u,v)=(u_{0},v_{0}) which are positive over a bounded region, representing the infected area of the disease in the initial stage. A spreading speed can be established for this model, which is the minimal speed of its traveling wave solutions; we refer to Zhao and Wang [34], Wu at al. [31] and references therein for research in this direction.

However, the approach described in the previous paragraph does not give the precise spreading front of the disease. This shortcoming can be addressed by considering the equations over a moving domain, resulting in a diffusive system with free boundaries. Such an approach was taken by Ahn et al. [2], who considered the following free boundary version of (1.2) (in one space dimension),

(1.3) {ut=d​ux​x−a​u+c​v,t>0,x∈(g(t),h(t)),vt=−b​v+G⁡(u),t>0,x∈(g(t),h(t)),u⁡(t,x)=v⁡(t,x)=0,t>0,x=g(t) or x=h(t),g(0)=−h0,g′(t)=−μux(t,g(t)),t>0,h(0)=h0,h′(t)=−μux(t,h(t)),t>0,u(0,x)=u0(x),v(0,x)=v0(x),x∈[−h0,h0],\begin{cases}u_{t}=du_{xx}-au+cv,&t>0,\ x\in(g(t),h(t)),\\ v_{t}=-bv+G(u),&t>0,\ x\in(g(t),h(t)),\\ u(t,x)=v(t,x)=0,&t>0,\ x=g(t)\text{\ or\ }x=h(t),\\ g(0)=-h_{0},\ g^{\prime}(t)=-\mu u_{x}(t,g(t)),&t>0,\\ h(0)=h_{0},\ h^{\prime}(t)=-\mu u_{x}(t,h(t)),&t>0,\\ u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\ v(0,x)=v_{0}(x),&x\in[-h_{0},h_{0}],\end{cases}

and proved a spreading-vanishing dichotomy for its long-time dynamical behaviour: The unique solution (u,v,g,h)(u,v,g,h) of (1.3) satisfies one of the following:

  • (i)

    Vanishing:

    limt→∞[h⁡(t)−g⁡(t)]<∞​ and ​limt→∞(‖u⁡(t,⋅)‖C⁡([g⁡(t),h⁡(t)])+‖v⁡(t,⋅)‖C⁡([g⁡(t),h⁡(t)]))=0\lim\limits_{t\to\infty}[h(t)-g(t)]<\infty\text{\ and\ }\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}(\|u(t,\cdot)\|_{C([g(t),h(t)])}+\|v(t,\cdot)\|_{C([g(t),h(t)])})=0;
  • (ii)

    Spreading:

    limt→∞[h⁡(t)−g⁡(t)]=∞​ and ​R0>1,limt→∞(u,v)=(K1,K2)​ locally uniformly in ​ℝ\lim\limits_{t\to\infty}[h(t)-g(t)]=\infty\text{\ and\ }R_{0}>1,\;\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}(u,v)=(K_{1},K_{2})\text{\ locally uniformly in\ }\mathbb{R},

where

(1.4) R0:=c​G′​(0)a​b,R_{0}:=\frac{cG^{\prime}(0)}{ab},

and (K1,K2)(K_{1},K_{2}) are uniquely determined by

G⁡(K1)=a​bc​K1,K2=G⁡(K1)b.G(K_{1})=\frac{ab}{c}K_{1},\;\;K_{2}=\frac{G(K_{1})}{b}.

Furthermore,

  • (i)

    if R0≤1R_{0}\leq 1, then vanishing happens;

  • (ii)

    if R0≥1+da​(π2​h0)2R_{0}\geq 1+\frac{d}{a}\big(\frac{\pi}{2h_{0}}\big)^{2}, then spreading happens;

  • (iii)

    if 1<R0<1+da​(π2​h0)21<R_{0}<1+\frac{d}{a}\big(\frac{\pi}{2h_{0}}\big)^{2}, then vanishing happens for small initial data (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}), and spreading happens for large initial data.

When spreading happens, the spreading speed of (1.3) was established in [33].

Note that in (1.2) and (1.3), the dispersal of the infectious agents is assumed to follow the rules of random diffusion, which is not realistic in general. This kind of dispersal may be better described by a nonlocal diffusion operator of the form

d​∫ℝJ⁡(x−y)​u​(t,y)​𝑑y−d​u​(t,x),d\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}J(x-y)u(t,y)dy-du(t,x),

which can capture short-range as well as long-range factors in the dispersal by choosing the kernel function JJ properly [1, 18].

The following nonlocal version of (1.2),

(1.5) {ut=d​∫ℝJ⁡(x−y)​u​(t,y)​dy−du−a​u+c​v,x∈ℝ,t>0,vt=−b​v+G⁡(u),x∈ℝ,t>0\begin{cases}u_{t}=d\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}J(x-y)u(t,y)dy-du-au+cv,&x\in\mathbb{R},\;t>0,\\ v_{t}=-bv+G(u),&x\in\mathbb{R},\;t>0\end{cases}

and its variations have been considered in several recent works; see, for example, Wang at al. [26], Zhang et al. [32], and the references therein.

However, the nonlocal version of (1.3) has not been considered so far. After the work of Du and Lin [9] for a logistic type local diffusion model, free boundary approaches to local diffusion problems similar to (1.3) have been investigated by many researchers recently; see, e.g., [7, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 27, 28, 29, 30] and the references therein. Extensions of these free boundary problems to their nonlocal diffusion counterparts have been slow due partly to the fact that the Stefan condition in these local diffusion models does not readily extend to the nonlocal problems.

Recently, Cao et al. [4] proposed a nonlocal version of the logistic model of [9], and successfully extended many basic results of [9] to the nonlocal model. In this paper, following the approach of [4], we propose and examine a nonlocal version of (1.3), which has the form

(1.6) {ut=d​∫g⁡(t)h⁡(t)J⁡(x−y)​u​(t,y)​dy−du−a​u+c​v,t>0,x∈(g(t),h(t)),vt=−b​v+G⁡(u),t>0,x∈(g(t),h(t)),u⁡(t,x)=v⁡(t,x)=0,t>0,x=g(t) or x=h(t),g′(t)=−μ∫g⁡(t)h⁡(t)∫−∞g⁡(t)J(x−y)u(t,x)dydx,t>0,h′​(t)=μ​∫g⁡(t)h⁡(t)∫h⁡(t)+∞J⁡(x−y)​u​(t,x)​dy​dx,t>0,−g(0)=h(0)=h0,u(0,x)=u0(x),v(0,x)=v0(x),x∈[−h0,h0].\begin{cases}u_{t}=d\displaystyle\int_{g(t)}^{h(t)}J(x-y)u(t,y)dy-du-au+cv,&t>0,\ x\in(g(t),h(t)),\\ v_{t}=-bv+G(u),&t>0,\ x\in(g(t),h(t)),\\ u(t,x)=v(t,x)=0,&t>0,\ x=g(t)\text{\ or\ }x=h(t),\\ g^{\prime}(t)=-\mu\displaystyle\int_{g(t)}^{h(t)}\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{g(t)}J(x-y)u(t,x)dydx,&t>0,\\ h^{\prime}(t)=\mu\displaystyle\int_{g(t)}^{h(t)}\displaystyle\int_{h(t)}^{+\infty}J(x-y)u(t,x)dydx,&t>0,\\ -g(0)=h(0)=h_{0},\ u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\ v(0,x)=v_{0}(x),&x\in[-h_{0},h_{0}].\end{cases}

Here the kernel function J:ℝ→ℝJ:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is assumed to satisfy

  1. (J):

    J∈C⁡(ℝ)∩L∞​(ℝ)J\in C(\mathbb{R})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}),  JJ is symmetric and nonnegative,   J⁡(0)>0,∫ℝJ⁡(x)​𝑑x=1J(0)>0,\ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}J(x)dx=1.

The parameters a,b,c,d,μa,\ b,\ c,\ d,\ \mu and h0h_{0} are positive constants. The initial functions u0​(x),v0​(x)u_{0}(x),v_{0}(x) satisfy

(1.7) u0,v0∈C⁡([−h0,h0]),u0​(±h0)=v0​(±h0)=0,u0,v0>0​ in ​(−h0,h0).u_{0},v_{0}\in C([-h_{0},h_{0}]),\ u_{0}(\pm h_{0})=v_{0}(\pm h_{0})=0,\ u_{0},v_{0}>0\text{\ in\ }(-h_{0},h_{0}).

As before, we assume GG satisfies (G1)-(G2). An example is G⁡(z)=α​z1+zG(z)=\alpha\frac{z}{1+z} with α∈(0,a​b/c)\alpha\in(0,ab/c).

In (1.6), the free boundary conditions

{h′​(t)=μ​∫g⁡(t)h⁡(t)∫h⁡(t)+∞J⁡(x−y)​u​(t,x)​𝑑y​𝑑x,g′(t)=−μ∫g⁡(t)h⁡(t)∫−∞g⁡(t)J(x−y)u(t,x)dydx,\begin{cases}\displaystyle h^{\prime}(t)=\mu\int_{g(t)}^{h(t)}\int_{h(t)}^{+\infty}J(x-y)u(t,x)dydx,\vskip 3.0pt plus 1.0pt minus 1.0pt\\ \displaystyle g^{\prime}(t)=-\mu\int_{g(t)}^{h(t)}\int_{-\infty}^{g(t)}J(x-y)u(t,x)dydx,\end{cases}

mean that the expanding rate of the range [g⁡(t),h⁡(t)][g(t),h(t)] is proportional to the outward flux of the population across the boundary of the range (see [4] for further explanations and justification).

The main results of this paper are the following theorems:

Theorem 1.1 (Global existence and uniqueness).

Suppose that (J) and (G1)-(G2) hold. Then for any given h0>0h_{0}>0 and u0​(x),v0​(x)u_{0}(x),v_{0}(x) satisfying (1.7), problem (1.6) admits a unique solution (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x),g⁡(t),h⁡(t))(u(t,x),v(t,x),g(t),h(t)) defined for all t>0t>0.

Theorem 1.2 (Spreading-vanishing dichotomy).

Let the conditions of Theorem 1.1 hold and (u,v,g,h)(u,v,g,h) be the unique solution of (1.6). Then one of the following alternatives must happen:

  • (i)

    Spreading: limt→∞[h⁡(t)−g⁡(t)]=∞\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}[h(t)-g(t)]=\infty ((and necessarily R0>1R_{0}>1)),

    limt→+∞(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))=(K1,K2)​ locally uniformly in ​ℝ.\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow+\infty}(u(t,x),v(t,x))=(K_{1},K_{2})\text{\ locally uniformly in\ }\mathbb{R}.
  • (ii)

    Vanishing: limt→∞(g⁡(t),h⁡(t))=(g∞,h∞)\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}(g(t),h(t))=(g_{\infty},h_{\infty}) is a finite interval, and

    limt→∞maxg⁡(t)≤x≤h⁡(t)⁡u⁡(t,x)=0​ and ​limt→∞maxg⁡(t)≤x≤h⁡(t)⁡v⁡(t,x)=0.\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}\max\limits_{g(t)\leq x\leq h(t)}u(t,x)=0\text{\ and\ }\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}\max\limits_{g(t)\leq x\leq h(t)}v(t,x)=0.

Let us recall that R0R_{0} is given by (1.4).

Theorem 1.3 (Spreading-vanishing criteria).

In Theorem 1.2, the dichotomy can be determined as follows:

  • (i)

    If R0≤1R_{0}\leq 1, then vanishing happens.

  • (ii)

    If R0≥1+daR_{0}\geq 1+\frac{d}{a}, then spreading happens.

  • (ii)

    If 1<R0<1+da1<R_{0}<1+\frac{d}{a}, then there exists l∗>0l^{*}>0 such that spreading happens when 2​h0≥l∗2h_{0}\geq l^{\ast}, and if 2​h0<l∗2h_{0}<l^{\ast}, then there exists μ∗>0\mu^{*}>0 such that spreading happens if and only if μ>μ∗\mu>\mu^{*}.

We note that l∗l^{*} depends only on (a,b,c,d,J)(a,b,c,d,J), which is determined by an eigenvalue problem (see (3.12)), but μ∗\mu^{*} depends also on the initial data.

Remark 1.4.

From part (ii) of Theorem 1.3, we see that if R0>1R_{0}>1 then for all small d>0d>0, spreading happens. This is very different from the local diffusion model (1.3), where in the corresponding case, the size of the initial population range 2​h02h_{0} (and the initial functions) also plays an important role.

Remark 1.5.

Very recently, Du, Li and Zhou [8] investigated the spreading speed of the nonlocal model in [4] and proved that the spreading may or may not have a finite speed, depending on whether a certain condition is satisfied by the kernel function JJ in the nonlocal diffusion term. We expect a similar result for (1.6), which will be considered in a future work.

In [12], some two species Lotka-Volterra models with nonlocal diffusion and free boundaries have been considered. There, nonlocal diffusion happens to both species, and the reaction/growth functions are also very different from (1.6) here. As a result, the techniques and results there are very different from this paper here.

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. In Section 2 we prove Theorem 1.1, namely, problem (1.6) has a unique solution defined for all t>0t>0. The long-time dynamical behaviour of (1.6) is investigated in Section 3, where Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 are proved.

This follows the idea in the proof of Lemma 3.8 in [4]. For example, if g∞=−∞g_{\infty}=-\infty but h∞<+∞h_{\infty}<+\infty, then we may argue as in the proof of Lemma 3.8 here to obtain h′​(t)≥ξ0>0h^{\prime}(t)\geq\xi_{0}>0 for all large tt, which yields a contradiction. ∎

Lemma 3.14.

Suppose θ>0\theta>0. If h∞−g∞=+∞h_{\infty}-g_{\infty}=+\infty, then

limt→∞(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))=(K1,K2)​ locally uniformly in ​ℝ.\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}(u(t,x),v(t,x))=(K_{1},K_{2})\text{\ locally uniformly in\ }\mathbb{R}.
Proof.

By Lemma 3.13, h∞−g∞=+∞h_{\infty}-g_{\infty}=+\infty implies that h∞=−g∞=+∞h_{\infty}=-g_{\infty}=+\infty. Then we can choose an increasing sequence {tn}\{t_{n}\} satisfying

limn→∞tn=+∞,λp​(ℒ(g⁡(tn),h⁡(tn))+θ)>0​ for ​n≥1.\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}t_{n}=+\infty,\ \lambda_{p}(\mathcal{L}_{(g(t_{n}),h(t_{n}))}+\theta)>0\text{\ for\ }n\geq 1.

Denote gn=g⁡(tn)g_{n}=g(t_{n}) and hn=h⁡(tn)h_{n}=h(t_{n}). Let (u¯n​(t,x),v¯n​(t,x))(\underline{u}_{n}(t,x),\underline{v}_{n}(t,x)) be the unique solution of

(3.15) {u¯t=d​∫gnhnJ2​(x−y)​u¯​(t,y)​dy−du¯−a​u¯+c​v¯,t>tn,x∈(gn,hn),v¯t=−b​v¯+G⁡(u¯),t>tn,x∈(gn,hn),u¯(tn,x)=u(tn,x),v¯(tn,x)=v(tn,x),x∈[gn,hn].\begin{cases}\underline{u}_{t}=d\displaystyle\int_{g_{n}}^{h_{n}}J_{2}(x-y)\underline{u}(t,y)dy-d\underline{u}-a\underline{u}+c\underline{v},&t>t_{n},\ x\in(g_{n},h_{n}),\\ \underline{v}_{t}=-b\underline{v}+G(\underline{u}),&t>t_{n},\ x\in(g_{n},h_{n}),\\ \underline{u}(t_{n},x)=u(t_{n},x),\ \underline{v}(t_{n},x)=v(t_{n},x),&x\in[g_{n},h_{n}].\end{cases}

Since λp​(ℒ(gn,hn)+θ)>0\lambda_{p}(\mathcal{L}_{(g_{n},h_{n})}+\theta)>0, it follows from Lemma 3.8 that (3.15) admits a unique positive steady state (U¯n​(x),V¯n​(x))(\underline{U}_{n}(x),\underline{V}_{n}(x)) and

limt→∞(u¯n​(t,x),v¯n​(t,x))=(U¯n​(x),V¯n​(x))​ uniformly in ​[gn,hn].\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}(\underline{u}_{n}(t,x),\underline{v}_{n}(t,x))=(\underline{U}_{n}(x),\underline{V}_{n}(x))\text{\ uniformly in\ }[g_{n},h_{n}].

By Corollary 3.6,

limn→∞(U¯n​(x),V¯n​(x))=(K1,K2)​ locally uniformly in ​ℝ.\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}(\underline{U}_{n}(x),\underline{V}_{n}(x))=(K_{1},K_{2})\text{\ locally uniformly in\ }\mathbb{R}.

Applying Lemma 3.1 and a simple comparison argument, we obtain

(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))≥(u¯n​(t,x),v¯n​(t,x))​ for ​t≥tn​ and ​x∈[gn,hn].(u(t,x),v(t,x))\geq(\underline{u}_{n}(t,x),\underline{v}_{n}(t,x))\text{\ for\ }t\geq t_{n}\text{\ and\ }x\in[g_{n},h_{n}].

Hence,

lim inft→∞(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))≥(K1,K2)​ locally uniformly in ​ℝ.\liminf\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}(u(t,x),v(t,x))\geq(K_{1},K_{2})\text{\ locally uniformly in\ }\mathbb{R}.

To complete the proof, it remains to show that

(3.16) lim supt→∞(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))≤(K1,K2)​ locally uniformly in ​ℝ.\limsup\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}(u(t,x),v(t,x))\leq(K_{1},K_{2})\text{\ locally uniformly in\ }\mathbb{R}.

Let (u^​(t),v^​(t))(\widehat{u}(t),\widehat{v}(t)) be the solution of

(3.17) {u′​(t)=−a​u​(t)+c​v​(t),t>0,v′​(t)=−b​v​(t)+G⁡(u⁡(t)),t>0,u(0)=∥u0∥∞,v(0)=∥v0∥∞.\begin{cases}u^{\prime}(t)=-au(t)+cv(t),&t>0,\\ v^{\prime}(t)=-bv(t)+G(u(t)),&t>0,\\ u(0)=\|u_{0}\|_{\infty},\ v(0)=\|v_{0}\|_{\infty}.&\end{cases}

By Lemma 3.2, we have u​(t,x)≤u^​(t)u(t,x)\leq\widehat{u}(t) and v​(t,x)≤v^​(t)v(t,x)\leq\widehat{v}(t) for t>0t>0 and x∈[g⁡(t),h⁡(t)]x\in[g(t),h(t)]. Since θ>0\theta>0 and hence R0>1R_{0}>1, the unique positive equilibrium (K1,K2)(K_{1},K_{2}) of (3.17) is globally attractive and so (u^​(t),v^​(t))→(K1,K2)(\widehat{u}(t),\widehat{v}(t))\rightarrow(K_{1},K_{2}) as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty, which clearly implies (3.16). ∎

Clearly Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 follow directly from Lemmas 3.4, 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12 and 3.14.
